newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch pledge to prepare Europe for new era.
newsitem.headline: Dutch pledge to prepare Europe for new era.

text.p: The Netherlands, assuming the European Union presidency, on Tuesday promised to build bridges between the 15 member states and with their non-EU partners and work to reform the bloc in preparation for the next century.
Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, outlining his plans after talks with European Commission President Jacques Santer, said that many big decisions on Europe's future lay ahead.

"We know a number of decisions will have to be taken... We are just three years away from the 21st century and Europe must do everything it possibly can if we are to meet the challenges of the new era," Kok told a news conference in The Hague.
"Over the next six months, The Netherlands...will do everything it can to make a strong and constructive contribution to this -- continuing to build the common European home.
"The Netherlands is highly motivated in achieving positive results...and looks forward with confidence to building this European home...a safe and happy home."
Santer, however, warned that the Dutch must come up with concrete achievements during their six-month presidency.
"This is the last chance...I believe the political will is there. The Dutch are pragmatic and inspired by the spirit of the (Union's) founding fathers."

Kok said the Dutch would adopt the attitude of former U.S. President John Kennedy. "No one should confine themselves simply to asking what Europe can do for us. The question is: what we together can do for our Europe, for our common future."
"The Europe of tomorrow is a safe, a social, a responsible and an undivided Europe. A Europe of, and for, its citizens."
Kok highlighted two key steps for Europe.
Firstly, it had to restructure ahead of embracing new members, primarily from the formerly-Communist Eastern Europe.
"This will involve the disappearance of the unnatural demarcation line that crossed Europe for half a century. We can take advantage of this historic opportunity to build a stable Europe," he said.
The Dutch hope to win agreement by the mid-June Amsterdam summit on landmark treaty reforms, setting the institutional framework for a workable bloc of up to 25 nations early in the next millennium.
This will involve tortuous negotiations on voting procedures, the number of Commission seats per member state and how to let some countries move quicker than others towards fuller integration.
"In a larger Union, flexibility is necessary to prevent one or more countries moving more slowly, stopping others from working together," Kok said. "But flexibility must not lead to fragmentation."
Secondly, the bloc had to make progress on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and complete the internal market -- a border-free area of some 370 million consumers.
"This is an essential building block if, in the long term, we are to have greater political cooperation," he added.
Kok said Ireland, which held the EU presidency for the second half of 1996, had provided a "very good basis" for the Dutch to work on.
"But in the months ahead, we may well have to narrow the focus and take decisions...inspired by political will."
He called for better policies on jobs and the environment and urged the bloc to improve its record on foreign policy.
"We must enhance our action together, we must enhance our credibility and, where possible, speak with a single voice."

"Europe cannot simply look in on itself...we must not just build bridges between the member states of today, and those of tomorrow, but rather we must build bridges to all four corners of the globe," he said, singling out current "problem" areas like the Middle East, the former Yugoslavia and Russia.
He also signalled a drive towards a "Citizen's Europe" -- enshrining freedom of movement and waging a common fight against organised crime, drug trafficking and racism.
